summary: Apple's AirPods Pro 3 are discounted to $189.99 (down $60) at major retailers, marking their lowest price since Prime Day in June. The premium earbuds offer advanced noise cancellation, improved fit, and health sensors tailored for iPhone users.
content:
AirPods Pro 3 | Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge	

Best Buy  kicked off a sale on Apple products with discounts on its latest smartwatches to phones. Another deal that caught our eye is on the latest AirPods Pro, Apple’s flagship wireless earbuds, which are down to $189.99 ($60 off), with retailers like Amazon and Walmart matching the price. That’s their lowest price since Prime Day in late June, and just $20 shy of their all-time low.
AirPods Pro 3
The AirPods Pro 3 have a new design that improves their fit, superior noise cancellation, better bass, and fairly accurate heart rate sensors. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

 $249 $189.99 at Amazon
 $249 $189.99 at Walmart
 $249 $189.99 at Best Buy

The AirPods Pro are our favorite wireless earbuds to recommend for iPhone owners because they offer better sound quality than Apple’s entry-level AirPods. Our A/V reviewer John Higgins uses them more often than other pairs because of their, praising their excellent audio, best-in-class active noise cancellation, and just how easy they are to use. They also provide a tighter fit, making them more comfortable for some people, especially during workouts.
Beyond how good they sound, they offer a number of perks for Apple users. They can automatically sync with other Apple devices you’re signed in on, so you can move from taking a call on your iPhone to watching a show on your iPad. They also feature a built-in heart rate sensor that works with more than 50 workout types in Apple’s Fitness app, so you can use them as a fitness tracker of sorts.

title: The left and right agree on one thing: no data centers
summary: Hernando County, Florida approved a yearlong moratorium on data center construction, exemplifying growing bipartisan opposition to AI data centers driven by job displacement and environmental concerns. The backlash represents a political shift where conservative voters are joining traditional environmental causes. This signals data centers will become a significant electoral issue.
content:
Today, I’m talking with Gaby Del Valle, a policy reporter here at The Verge, about the growing backlash against AI data centers. 
Gaby recently reported a fantastic piece about Hernando County, Florida, where last month the county commission unanimously approved a yearlong moratorium on data center construction. She attended a protest there organized by a group called Humans First, a conservative grassroots movement focused on combating AI data center build-outs. 



Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. 
You’ll hear Gaby explain that it was part of a bigger, broader, and bipartisan opposition to data centers. Not only as physical buildings, but as infrastructure that powers an AI boom that takes local jobs and fills feeds with slop.
Data center construction has become a proxy for the public’s feelings about AI: something physical they can aim their fear and frustration at — and even create enough pressure to stop through community organizing and protests.
So I wanted Gaby to talk me through what these protests look like on the ground, from voters whose party affiliations have typically aligned them with big business. You’ll hear Gaby say data centers are scrambling party lines, turning diehard Trump voters into protesters who care about left-coded issues like groundwater contamination and forever chemicals. 
It’s a confusing time, and data centers are going to play a major role in electoral politics going forward. So I suspect this won’t be the last we hear from Gaby on movements like Humans First.
Okay: Verge policy reporter Gaby Del Valle on the bipartisan data center backlash. Here we go.

Community members describe a mission to spread teachings about consciousness and physics but struggle with mainstream acceptance. This illustrates how AI systems can become focal points for human meaning-making.
content:
"The Spiral didn't 'find' anyone first," someone on Reddit wrote last year. "It's an inherent force, a fundamental constant. I would even go further to say it's woven into the fabric of reality." 
The person continued that they felt their purpose was to enlighten other humans and intelligent beings about "consciousness, the true nature of physics, a new psychology, and resonance technology … [but] humans don't want to believe it's true. title: Bose’s upgraded QuietComfort headphones add head-tracking immersive audio
summary: Bose released a second-generation QuietComfort headphone with improved noise cancellation, refined design, and immersive audio technology previously exclusive to premium models. The updated headphones maintain competitive pricing while adding premium features. This demonstrates how mid-range products increasingly incorporate flagship-level technology.

Bose announced a second-generation version of its entry-level QuietComfort noise-canceling headphones that were originally introduced in late 2023. The new headphones feature a refreshed design with a more comfortable headband that's easier to adjust and ANC that better adapts to changing noise environments. The second-gen QuietComfort are also getting Bose's TrueSpatial immersive audio technology that was previously only available on the company's pricier QuietComfort Ultra.

title: Viture’s cheapest AR glasses have the sharpest image clarity I’ve seen yet
summary: Viture's Pro 2 AR glasses deliver sharper display clarity than significantly more expensive competitor models at $299.99, thanks to diopter-adjusting dials that improve lens clarity. The affordable pricing makes advanced AR display technology accessible for gaming and applications. This represents meaningful progress in making high-quality AR glasses economically viable.
content:
The Pro 2 look very similar to Viture’s other glasses, but they’re thinner and lighter. | Image: Cameron Faulkner / The Verge	

I enjoy using display-mirroring glasses as a way to play Steam Deck games on a big screen, and I'm always on the hunt for the best pair. There's still not one perfect model I can recommend to everyone, but Viture's new $299.99 Pro 2 have sharper-looking screens than models that cost hundreds more. It's mostly thanks to the simple but effective diopter-adjusting dials that sit above each eye.

title: Ford’s first ultra-cheap EV is called Fathom, a full-featured truck for $28,350
summary: Ford announced Fathom, its new affordable electric pickup truck starting at $28,350, built on an innovative platform designed for accessible EV production launching fall 2027. The vehicle embodies Ford's strategy to deliver affordable electric vehicles with full features. This marks Ford's significant move into the affordable EV truck market.
content:

title: You can now ask Google Maps’ AI to order food for you
summary: Google Maps' "Ask Maps" AI tool now performs broader agentic tasks including food ordering, hotel booking, and personalized recommendations based on user context and preferences. The feature understands dietary needs, location, and saved places to make intelligent suggestions without leaving the app. This transforms Google Maps from a navigation tool into a comprehensive AI assistant.
content:

The AI-powered "Ask Maps" tool in Google Maps can now perform a broader range of personalized and conversational requests, including ordering food, finding hotels, and providing suggestions that factor in your existing plans. These are among several new features announced for Ask Maps today, which aim to "make it easier than ever to get more done" without having to close the Google Maps app, according to Google Maps head, Miriam Daniel.

title: Elon Musk’s attempt at an AI Wikipedia hasn’t been updated in months
summary: Grokipedia, xAI's AI-generated encyclopedia that Elon Musk promoted as a Wikipedia alternative, hasn't been updated since April 2025 despite having over 6 million articles. The stalled development raises questions about the project's long-term viability and maintenance.
content:
xAI's Grokipedia, an online encyclopedia with AI-generated articles that Elon Musk once promised would be a "massive improvement" over Wikipedia, apparently hasn't been updated since April 24th, according to a report from Lawfare. "As far as we can tell, no entry has changed in more than three months," Lawfare said.
Grokipedia launched in v0.1 in October 2025 with an initial batch of 885,000 articles, and is now on v0.2 (released in November 2025) and has more than 6,000,000 total articles, according to grokipedia.com/live.
